config.title: Utility Types

intro.title: Utility Types
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays a user profile card. You will learn how to use TypeScript utility types like `Pick` and `Omit` to create flexible and reusable type definitions. The main technologies involved are React for the UI and TypeScript for type safety. By the end, you'll understand how utility types help you manage and transform object types efficiently in your projects.
intro.usecase: Utility types are essential for managing complex data structures in real-world React applications. In e-commerce dashboards, they help create filtered views of product data without modifying the original datasets. When building user profile forms, utility types ensure type safety when extracting or omitting sensitive fields like passwords. They're also crucial in admin panels where developers need to create read-only versions of editable data models for audit logs.

objectives: Implement utility types to transform existing object types in TypeScript
Apply the Partial utility type to make all properties of an object optional
Construct new types using the Pick utility to select specific properties
Configure the Readonly utility to prevent modification of object properties
Update type definitions using the Omit utility to exclude specific properties
Integrate the Record utility to create mapped types with specified keys and values
Manipulate union types using the Exclude and Extract utilities

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing from a package
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty fragment.
steps.hint: Define the component using either a function declaration or arrow function. Return React.Fragment shorthand <> </>.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create your App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named App and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named App that returns <> </>.

steps.title: Initialize user data state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'userData' initialized with a sample user object containing name, age, and email properties.
steps.hint: The useState hook returns an array with the current state and a setter function. Initialize it with an object like { name: 'John', age: 30, email: 'john@example.com' }.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with an object
const [product, setProduct] = useState({ name: 'Laptop', price: 999, inStock: true });
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component should have a userData state variable initialized with a user object containing name, age, and email properties.
successCriteria: userData state is declared using useState and initialized with an object containing name, age, and email properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track with useState, but make sure userData is initialized with an object containing name, age, and email properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState to create a state variable named 'userData' initialized with an object like { name: 'John', age: 30, email: 'john@example.com' }.

steps.title: Define updateUserData handler
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named updateUserData that takes a newData parameter and updates the userData state with the new values.
steps.hint: Use the setUserData function from useState to update the state with the newData parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The updateUserData function is defined and ready to update the userData state when called.
successCriteria: The updateUserData function is defined, takes a newData parameter, and calls setUserData with newData.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your updateUserData function takes a newData parameter and calls setUserData with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The updateUserData function isn't defined correctly. It should take a newData parameter and update the state using setUserData.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: In your App component's return statement, replace the current `null` with a `<div>` container that contains an `<h1>` heading with the text 'User Profile'.
steps.hint: Return a JSX structure with a div wrapper and an h1 heading inside.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a div container with an h1 heading displaying 'User Profile'.
successCriteria: The App component returns a div containing an h1 with the text 'User Profile'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a div with an h1 heading inside, and the heading text is exactly 'User Profile'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component should return a div container with an h1 heading 'User Profile'.

steps.title: Display current user data
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your App component, add a <div> with a heading 'Current User Data' and two paragraphs that display the current name and email values from the userData state.
steps.hint: Access the state values using userData.name and userData.email inside curly braces within the paragraphs.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying state values in JSX

Current Data

Name: {someState.name}

Email: {someState.email}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a heading 'Current User Data' with two paragraphs displaying the current name and email values (initially empty strings).
successCriteria:
A
contains an

with text 'Current User Data' and two

elements that render userData.name and userData.email.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have a heading and two paragraphs that show the name and email from the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UI doesn't show the current user data as expected. Check that you added the heading and paragraphs with the correct state values.

steps.title: Add update button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Update User' and wire its onClick event to call the updateUserData handler function.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick={updateUserData} and include the text content 'Update User'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with click handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click Me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Update User' appears in the UI, and clicking it will trigger the updateUserData handler (though the handler is not yet defined).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the button has the exact text 'Update User' and the onClick attribute is set to updateUserData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or click handler is missing. Add a <button> element with onClick={updateUserData} and the text 'Update User'.

steps.title: Add reset button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a second button with the text 'Reset User' and wire its onClick event to the resetUserData handler.
steps.hint: Place the button after the existing update button. Use the onClick prop and pass the resetUserData function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with a click handler
<button onClick={handleReset}>Reset</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A second button labeled 'Reset User' appears next to the 'Update User' button, and clicking it will trigger the resetUserData handler.
successCriteria: A <button> element with text 'Reset User' and onClick={resetUserData} is added to the JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check the text or onClick prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reset button is missing or not properly wired to the handler.

steps.title: Add explanatory text about utility patterns
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph below the reset button that explains how this pattern demonstrates utility concepts for managing and transforming data in JavaScript.
steps.hint:
Add a

element with text that connects the state management and handlers you've implemented to utility patterns in JavaScript.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: explanatory paragraph about a pattern

This pattern shows how we can use functions to transform and manage data consistently.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph appears below the reset button explaining how the state management and handler functions demonstrate utility patterns for data transformation.
successCriteria: The paragraph explains how the pattern demonstrates utility concepts for managing and transforming data in JavaScript.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but make sure it specifically explains how this pattern demonstrates utility concepts for managing and transforming data in JavaScript.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph is missing or doesn't explain how this pattern demonstrates utility concepts for managing and transforming data. Try adding a clear explanation below the reset button.
